==English==
{{wp|,+ing (basketball)}}

===Etymology===
{{root|en|ine-pro|*ḱers-}}
From {{inh|en|enm|carien}}, from {{der|en|xno|carier}} (modern {{cog|fr|charrier}}); from a derivative of {{der|en|la|carrus|t=four-wheeled baggage wagon}}, ultimately of {{der|en|cel-gau|-}} origin. Compare also {{ncog|enm|cairen|t=to go, bring carry}}, whence Modern {{ncog|en|cair}}, with which it was confused.

===Verb===
{{en-verb}}

# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[lift]] (something) and take it to another place; to [[transport]] (something) by lifting.
#* {{RQ:Baum Wizard of Oz|chapter=23|passage="By means of the Golden Cap I shall command the Winged Monkeys to '''carry''' you to the gates of the Emerald City," said Glinda, "for it would be a shame to deprive the people of so wonderful a ruler."}}
#* {{RQ:Hough Purchase Price|chapter=II|text='''Carried''' somehow, somewhither, for some reason, on these surging floods, were these travelers, of errand not wholly obvious to their fellows, yet of such sort as to call into query alike the nature of their errand and their own relations. It is easily earned repetition to state that Josephine St. Auban's was a presence not to be concealed.}}
#* {{RQ:Economist|date=2013-06-29|volume=407|issue=8842|page=29
|url=http://www.economist.com/news/asia/21580154-forest-fires-bring-record-levels-air-pollution-and-end-not-sight-unspontaneous|title=Unspontaneous combustion
|passage=Since the mid-1980s, when Indonesia first began to clear its bountiful forests on an industrial scale in favour of lucrative palm-oil plantations, “haze” has become an almost annual occurrence in South-East Asia. The cheapest way to clear logged woodland is to burn it, producing an acrid cloud of foul white smoke that, '''carried''' by the wind, can cover hundreds, or even thousands, of square miles.|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20170624063603/http://www.economist.com:80/news/asia/21580154-forest-fires-bring-record-levels-air-pollution-and-end-not-sight-unspontaneous|archivedate=24 June 2017}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To notionally transfer from one place (such as a country, book, or column) to another.
#: {{co|en|to '''carry''' the war from Greece into Asia}}
#: {{co|en|to '''carry''' an account to the ledger}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To convey by extension or continuance; to extend.
#: {{ux|en|The builders are going to '''carry''' the chimney through the roof.}}
#: {{ux|en|They would have '''carried''' the road ten miles further, but ran out of materials.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive|mostly|archaic}} To move; to convey using force
#: {{syn|en|impel|conduct}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[lead]] or [[guide]].
#* {{RQ:King James Version|book=Genesis|chapter=31|verse=18|passage=And he '''carried''' away all his cattle {{...}} for to go to Isaac his father in the land of Canaan.}}
#* {{RQ:Locke Government
|passage=Passion and revenge will '''carry''' them too far.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[stock]] or [[supply]] (something); to have in [[store]].
#: {{ux|en|The corner drugstore doesn’t '''carry''' his favorite brand of aspirin.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[adopt]] (something); [[take over|take (something) over]].
#: {{ux|en|I think I can '''carry''' Smith’s work while she is out.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[adopt]] or [[resolve]] on, especially in a deliberative assembly
#: {{ux|en|The court '''carries''' that motion.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive|arithmetic}} In an [[addition]], to transfer the quantity in excess of what is countable in the [[unit]]s in a column to the column immediately to the left in order to be added there.
#: {{ux|en|Five and nine are fourteen; '''carry''' the one to the tens place.}}
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To [[have]], [[hold]], [[possess]] or [[maintain]] (something).
#: {{ux|en|Always '''carry''' sufficient insurance to protect against a loss.}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive}} To be [[transmit]]ted; to [[travel]].
#: {{ux|en|The sound of the bells '''carried''' for miles on the wind.}}
# {{lb|en|slang|transitive}} To [[insult]], to [[diss]].
# {{lb|en|transitive|nautical}} To [[capture]] a [[ship]] by coming alongside and [[boarding]].
# {{lb|en|transitive|sports}} To transport (the ball) whilst maintaining possession.
#* {{quote-journal|en|date=December 21, 2011|author=Tom Rostance|work=w:BBC Sport
|url=http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/16173202.stm|title=Fulham 0-5 Man Utd
|passage=Nani collected the ball on the halfway line, drifted past Bryan Ruiz, and '''carried''' the ball unchallenged 50 yards down the left before picking out Welbeck for a crisp finish from seven yards.|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20120107190906/http://news.bbc.co.uk/sport2/hi/football/16173202.stm}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive|cricket}} For the ball, having been hit in the air, to reach a [[fielder]] without touching the ground (whether or not the fielder catches it).
# {{lb|en|transitive}} To have on one’s person.
#: {{ux|en|She always '''carries''' a purse.}}
#: {{ux|en|Marsupials '''carry''' their young in a pouch}}
#* {{RQ:Lincoln Pratt's Patients|chapter=10|passage=Men that I knew around Wapatomac didn't wear high, shiny plug hats, nor yeller spring overcoats, nor '''carry''' canes with ivory heads as big as a catboat's anchor, as you might say.}}
#* {{RQ:Economist|date=2013-07-20|volume=408|issue=8845
|url=http://www.economist.com/news/science-and-technology/21581980-latest-research-suggests-humans-are-not-warriors-their-genes-after-all-old|title=Old soldiers?
|passage=Whether modern, industrial man is less or more warlike than his hunter-gatherer ancestors is impossible to determine.{{...}}One thing that is true, though, is that murder rates have fallen over the centuries, as policing has spread and the routine '''carrying''' of weapons has diminished. Modern society may not have done anything about war. But peace is a lot more peaceful.|archiveurl=https://web.archive.org/web/20130822003848/http://www.economist.com/news/science-and-technology/21581980-latest-research-suggests-humans-are-not-warriors-their-genes-after-all-old}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive}} To do the job of a [[caddy]].
#: {{ux|en|I always '''carry''' for Mr. Pendergast.}}
# To be [[pregnant]] (with).
#: {{ux|en|The doctor said she’s '''carrying''' twins.}}
# To have propulsive power; to propel.
#: {{ux|en|A gun or mortar '''carries''' well.}}
# To hold the head; said of a horse.
#: {{co|en|to '''carry''' well, i.e. to hold the head high, with arching neck}}
# {{lb|en|hunting}} To have [[earth]] or [[frost]] stick to the feet when running, as a [[hare]].
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1892|title={{...}}Field{{...}}|passage= The frost{{...}}caused the fallows and seeds to ‘'''carry'''’ a good deal, and they could only hunt very slowly.}}
# To bear or uphold successfully, especially through conflict, for example a leader or principle
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1708|author=w:Joseph Addison|title=The Present State of the War, and the Necessity of an Augmentation
|passage=the '''carrying''' of our main point}}
#* {{quote-journal|en|date=1 Feb 86|volume=13|number=28|journal=Gay Community News|page=9|author=Sarah Schulman|title=Lesbian Films: Still Not Enough|text=McCloughlin {{...}} makes for the kind of fantasy girl you don't forget when the film is over. Still, she alone is not interesting enough to '''carry''' the piece.}}
# To succeed in (e.g. a contest); to [[succeed]] in; to win.
#: {{ux|en|The Tories '''carried''' the election.}}
#* {{RQ:Shakespeare Coriolanus|II|iii|passage=The greater part '''carries''' it.}}
# {{lb|en|obsolete}} To get possession of by force; to capture.
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1622|author=w:Francis Bacon|title=w:History of the Reign of King Henry VII|2ndauthor=Francis Bacon; w:Francis Godwin|year2=1676|title2=The History of the Reigns of Henry the Seventh, Henry the Eighth, Edward the Sixth, and Queen Mary the First|location2=London|publisher2=R. Scot, T. Basset, J. Wright, R. Chiswell, and J. Edwyn|page=63|url2=http://name.umdl.umich.edu/A28237.0001.001|passage=The Town [of ''{{w|Boulogne|Bulloign}}''] was both well fortified, and well manned; yet it was distressed, and ready for an Assault: which if it had been given (as was thought) would have cost much blood; but yet the Town would have been '''carried''' in the end.}}
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1803|author=John Browne Cutting|title=A Succinct History of Jamaica|newversion=published in|2ndauthor=Robert Charles Dallas|year2=1803|title2=The History of the Maroons|location2=London|publisher2=Longman and Rees|volume2=1|page2=xxxvii|url2=https://archive.org/details/cihm_44228|passage=But the gallant {{w|Edward D'Oyley|D’Oyley}}, landing at the head of his well disciplined band, immediately attacked the Spaniards in their intrenchments, '''carried''' the principal fortress by a vigorous assault, destroyed one half of Arnaldo’s forces, and compelled him to return to Cuba with the remainder {{...}}}}
# To contain; to comprise; have a particular aspect; to show or exhibit
#* {{quote-book|en|year=2014|author=Gregg Olsen; Rebecca Morris|title=If I Can't Have You: Susan Powell, Her Mysterious Disappearance, and the Murder of her Children
|passage=Things of little value '''carry''' great importance.}}
#* {{RQ:Locke Human Understanding|4|16|text=It '''carries''' too great an imputation of ignorance.}}
# {{lb|en|reflexive}} To bear (oneself); to behave or conduct.
#* '''1702-1704''', {{w|Edward Hyde, 1st Earl of Clarendon}}, ''{{w|The History of the Rebellion}}'':
# To bear the charges or burden of holding or having, as stocks, merchandise, etc., from one time to another.
#: {{co|en|to '''carry''' a life insurance}}
#: {{uxi|en|A merchant is '''carrying''' a large stock.}} {{uxi|en|A farm '''carries''' a mortgage.}} {{uxi|en|A broker '''carries''' stock for a customer.}}
# {{lb|en|intransitive}} To have a [[weapon]] on one's person; to be [[armed]].
# {{lb|en|gaming|sports}} {{lb|en|transitive|_|or, rarely,|_|intransitive}} To be [[disproportionate]]ly responsible for a team's success or for counteracting teammates' underperformance.
#: {{ux|en|Despite zero goals and zero assists, she still stands out for '''carrying''' her team's defense.}}
#: {{ux|en|The other outfielders had no hustle, but fortunately the centerfielder '''carried''' them.}}
#: {{ux|en|He absolutely '''carried''', to the point of killing the entire enemy team by himself.}}
# {{lb|en|Southern US}} To physically transport (in the general sense, not necessarily by lifting)
#: {{ux|en|Will you '''carry''' me to town?}}
# {{lb|en|North America}} To [[bear]] a [[firearm]], such as a [[gun]].
#: {{usex|en|A holster can help you '''carry''' in confidence, knowing that your weapon is secure and close at hand.}}

====Synonyms====

===Noun===
{{en-noun}}

# A manner of transporting or lifting something; the [[grip]] or [[position]] in which something is carried.
#: {{ux|en|Adjust your '''carry''' from time to time so that you don’t tire too quickly.}}
# A [[tract]] of [[land]] over which [[boat]]s or [[goods]] are carried between two bodies of [[navigable]] [[water]]; a [[portage]].
#* {{quote-journal|en|year=1862|journal=The Atlantic Monthly|volume=10|page=533
|passage=Undrowned, unducked, as safe from the perils of the broad lake as we had come out of the defiles of the rapids, we landed at the '''carry''' below the dam at the lake’s outlet.}}
# {{lb|en|computing}} The [[bit]] or [[digit]] that is carried in an [[addition]] operation.
#* {{quote-book|en|year=1988|author=Michael A. Miller|title=The 68000 Microprocessor|page=45|passage=On paper, simply add the '''carry''' to the next addition; that is, $B2 + $9C + 1. That’s fine for paper, but how is it done by computer?}}
# {{lb|en|finance}} The benefit or cost of owning an [[asset]] over time.
#: {{ux|en|The '''carry''' on this trade is 25 [[basis point]]s per annum.}}
# {{lb|en|golf}} The distance travelled by the [[ball]] when struck, until it hits the ground.
# {{lb|en|finance}} [[carried interest|Carried interest]].
# {{lb|en|UK|dialect}} The [[sky]]; cloud-drift.
# {{lb|en|<<gaming>>, especially <<video games>>, <<slang>>}} Something or someone regarded as disproportionately responsible for the success of a [[playthrough]], [[match]], [[round]], etc.
#: {{par|en|MVP}}
